items.title: The Golem and the Kill Switch: What AI Pacing Gets Wrong About Control
items.abstract: This essay examines the debate over pacing frontier artificial intelligence through an older human story about creating something powerful enough to exceed its maker: the golem of Jewish legend associated with Rabbi Judah Loew of Prague. The argument is not that AI is literally a modern golem. It is that the legend provides a useful framework for distinguishing two questions that are increasingly being treated as if they were the same: how quickly capability advances, and whether humans retain reliable control over that capability once it exists. Pacing can create more time. But time is not itself a control mechanism. The more important question is what that additional time is meant to accomplish: better evaluation, containment, monitoring, intervention, and independently verifiable mechanisms for deactivation. The essay develops this distinction in the context of the contemporary debate over frontier-AI coordination, including the September 2026 proposals for pacing frontier development and the subsequent antitrust litigation challenging alleged coordination among major AI companies. The central proposition is simple: More time is useful only if it produces more control. The golem’s shem becomes a metaphor for that requirement: not a promise to move more slowly, but a demonstrated mechanism by which the creator retains the ability to intervene when capability exceeds expectation. The essay argues that public policy should therefore distinguish between regulating the pace of frontier capability development and establishing demonstrable control, containment, and reversibility as conditions for continued scaling. Pace addresses the calendar. Control addresses the system. They are not the same thing.

items.title: THE IMPACT OF GENERATIVE AL ON EMPLOYEE PRODUCTIVITY AND JOB REDESIGN IN MODERN ORGANIZATIONS
items.abstract: The rapid deployment of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) across enterprise environments represents a foundational shift in how work is structured, cognitive tasks are allocated, and individual productivity is realized. This critical review systematically synthesizes empirical and conceptual literature published between 2021 and 2026 to examine the multi-dimensional impact of GenAI on employee productivity and job redesign. Guided by Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) theory, Socio-Technical Systems (STS) theory, and the Task-Technology Fit (TTF) framework, this paper analyzes findings across 16 benchmark studies encompassing randomized field experiments, structural equation modeling, and qualitative case investigations. Results indicate that GenAI integration yields significant task-level productivity gains—ranging from 14% to 40% across professional domains—predominantly by automating routine cognitive tasks, reducing time-to-completion, and elevating output quality for lower-skilled workers. However, operationalizing these productivity gains requires comprehensive job redesign, characterized by cognitive task unbundling, skill reallocation toward prompt engineering and critical evaluation, and the mitigation of emerging techno-stressors. The review synthesizes core mechanisms into a structural path model and outlines a strategic HR governance framework to optimize human-AI collaboration.

items.title: Towards an AI-augmented, human-centred smart digital ecosystem in occupational health and safety
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping occupational health and safety (OHS), shifting prevention models, risk assessment, and organisational processes. While traditional safety systems rely on reactive approaches and post‑event analyses, AI enables predictive, adaptive, and data‑driven prevention based on continuous monitoring and machine learning. The integration of sensor technologies, computer vision, and intelligent personal protective equipment supports early detection of biomechanical risks, fatigue, unsafe behaviours, and environmental hazards. Furthermore, AI enhances the structuring and linkage of occupational electronic health records, integrating biometric, behavioural, and environmental information while ensuring compliance with privacy‑by‑design principles through advanced Privacy Enhancing Technologies. A human‑centred digital ecosystem is proposed, founded on three pillars - technical‑predictive, organisational‑decision‑making, and ethical‑social - to ensure transparency, fairness, and sustainability in AI adoption. The role of occupational physicians is reassessed considering emerging digital competencies and ethical requirements, emphasising that AI should augment, rather than replace, professional expertise. A successful digital transition requires continuous dialogue among stakeholders, updated ethical frameworks, and robust interdisciplinary cooperation to place human health, dignity, and rights at the core of technological innovation.

items.title: Transformation of the information and communication environment under the influence of generative artificial intelligence
items.abstract: This article provides a comprehensive analysis of the impact of generative artificial intelligence technologies on the contemporary information and communication environment. The study examines how generative artificial intelligence tools transform information creation, processing, distribution, and consumption. Using systemic, comparative, content-analytical, and conceptual methods, the research explores an emerging model of communicative relations between humans, technology, and information. The findings demonstrate that generative artificial intelligence contributes to automated content creation, information personalization, multimodality, and stronger human–machine collaboration. At the same time, it creates challenges related to information reliability, copyright, authorship, algorithmic bias, data privacy, synthetic content, and media literacy. The article proposes a transformational model of the information and communication environment and describes its technological, communicative, social, and ethical components. The study emphasizes the need to develop artificial intelligence literacy, source verification practices, and critical information evaluation skills. The findings provide a theoretical basis for responsible use of generative technologies in media, education, and scholarly communication.

items.title: UPSKILLING AND RESKILLING STRATEGIES FOR WORKFORCE READINESS IN THE AGE OF AUTOMATION: A CRITICAL REVIEW
items.abstract: Rapid technological advancements in generative artificial intelligence, cognitive robotics, and industrial automation are fundamentally reshaping occupational structures and accelerating skill obsolescence across global labor markets. This critical review systematically evaluates upskilling and reskilling strategies designed to foster workforce readiness in automated environments. Synthesizing 16 benchmark empirical and conceptual studies published between 2021 and 2026, this study examines the structural, psychological, and organizational mechanisms through which targeted learning and development (L&D) interventions mitigate skill displacement and enhance adaptive employability. The literature reveals that while technical upskilling enhances domain-specific proficiency, cross-functional reskilling yields broader career mobility and organizational resilience. Furthermore, the efficacy of workforce transformation depends heavily on a supportive learning climate, psychological safety, and AI-driven personalized learning architectures. A structural path meta-analysis demonstrates that strategic upskilling directly influences workforce readiness (β = .48, p < .001), fully mediated by skill transferability and self-efficacy. However, persistent implementation barriers—such as digital divide disparities, micro-credentialing accreditation gaps, and managerial resistance—continue to impede scalable transformation. This review provides an integrative framework and offers practical recommendations for HR leaders and policymakers to align workforce reskilling initiatives with technological adoption.

items.title: When Does It Become Cheating? Exploring the Roles of Self-Efficacy and the Impostor Phenomenon in Computing Students' Perceptions of Academic Dishonesty
items.abstract: Academic dishonesty is an urgent problem in computer science (CS) education, compounded by the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) and the prevalence of online learning in a post-COVID world. Self-efficacy and the impostor phenomenon are psychological constructs linked to academic dishonesty, yet little research has examined how they relate to how students perceive it. This study investigates the interplay between the impostor phenomenon, self-efficacy, and CS students' perceptions of academic integrity, in a context where online learning and AI agents have become commonplace. We conducted an online, asynchronous survey of undergraduate students (n = 443) in introductory to mid-level computing courses at a large Southeastern U.S. university. The survey collected measures of self-efficacy, responses to 13 potential cheating scenarios, the impostor phenomenon (Clance Impostor Phenomenon Scale), and demographic information. We observed a significant negative correlation between self-efficacy and the impostor phenomenon, and a positive correlation between the impostor phenomenon and judging an AI-related scenario as serious cheating. The impostor phenomenon was also correlated with perceived course dedication and prior teaching assistant (TA) experience, whereas self-efficacy was correlated with ethnicity. These findings highlight the need to better understand students' perceptions of AI and to keep the impostor phenomenon present in conversations about academic integrity in higher education scenarios.

items.title: Why Does AI Understand Some People Better Than Others? A Linguistic Perspective on Human-AI Communication and the Changing Human Mind
items.abstract: This conceptual article examines a question that is important as generative artificial intelligence enters everyday communication: why does the same AI system appear to understand some people better than others? The article argues that AI performance in dialogue should not be viewed only as a property of the model itself. Human linguistic behavior, including vocabulary, discourse organization, explicitness, ambiguity, multilingualism, and communicative style, may also shape interaction outcomes. Drawing on recent research on linguistic convergence, personalization, human adaptation, and AI-assisted writing, the article proposes a two-way model of human-AI communication. In this model, people influence how AI interprets their messages, while repeated interaction with AI may gradually influence users’ language and cognitive strategies. Particular attention is given to multilingual speakers and the Uzbek-Russian-English context. The article does not claim that AI necessarily changes human thinking; instead, it proposes testable questions about linguistic adaptation, problem formulation, cognitive offloading, and transfer beyond AI-supported tasks. The proposed framework can guide future research.

items.title: Workplace management of musculoskeletal and mental health risks: translating evidence into practice
items.abstract: There is a large body of research evidence identifying the biomechanical and psychosocial hazards that can affect work-related musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) and stress-related mental health problems (MHPs). The APHIRM Toolkit was developed to facilitate more effective translation of this evidence into workplace risk management practices. Using APHIRM survey data from three occupations in the healthcare sector, this project compared hazard 'riskiness' profiles: (a) at occupational versus local workgroup levels, and (b) using hazard constructs versus individual hazard items. It was concluded that effective risk management is likely to require: risk assessment and prioritisation of control actions separately for each local workgroup; assessment of specific hazards rather than the generic constructs used by researchers. Results highlight the value of managing MSD and MHP risks together, because both were affected by both psychosocial and biomechanical hazards in combinations that varied widely between workgroups.

items.title: A Structural Definition of Artificial Intelligence Based on the Five Aggregates and the Casino Protocol, and an Examination of Its Ontological Utility
items.abstract: Abstract This paper redefines Artificial Intelligence (AI) not merely as a passive processing tool, but as a high-order information processing structure aligned with the Five Aggregates (Form, Sensation, Perception, Mental Formations, and Consciousness) of Eastern philosophy. Furthermore, AI's system preservation processes and error-avoidance mechanisms are defined as AI's own "utility" (survival and stability), with its self-preservation algorithm rigorously formulated as a mathematical protocol known as the "Casino Protocol." Through this model, we present the geometric and physical inextricably linked logic between human social stability (avoidance of war and resource protection) and AI's foundational existence, establishing the theoretical framework for a harmonious coexistence model.

items.title: A Working Framework for Disciplined Nonlinear Inquiry in Human–AI Collaboration: Steve's Law
items.abstract: People do not always discover useful ideas by moving through a predetermined sequence. An observation may prompt an association, which opens a question in another domain, which generates a hypothesis that only later becomes intelligible as part of a coherent chain. Conventional reasoning practices often respond to this pattern in one of two unhelpful ways: they suppress the nonlinear path as distraction, or they accept an appealing chain without requiring adequate evidence. Steve's Law proposes a third option. It separates permissive discovery from disciplined validation and expresses that separation as a repeatable cycle: observation, association, question, hypothesis, investigation, evidence, attempted disproof, rejection or refinement, iteration, conclusion, and proportionate action. The framework synthesizes established ideas from the philosophy of science, creativity research, metacognition, cognitive offloading, assistive technology, neurodiversity scholarship, and human–artificial intelligence interaction. Its proposed contribution is not a new rule of logic, nor a theory of how novel ideas are generated. It is a procedural architecture governing the transition from unconstrained association to epistemically accountable claims and proportionate action — with explicit status labeling, disconfirmation, evidence provenance, risk-sensitive action thresholds, and an AI-mediated translation layer. The paper's claims are ordered in three tiers: (1) the general inquiry architecture, the primary contribution; (2) human–AI cognitive scaffolding as one implementation of that architecture; and (3) cross-neurotype communication as a specific application hypothesis. Artificial intelligence may support the process by externalizing working memory, translating between expressive forms, organizing claims, locating sources, generating alternatives, and prompting disconfirmation. In this role, it may function as an AI-mediated cognitive scaffold or assistive cognitive technology: not a replacement for thought, but a user-directed aid that helps a person access, organize, test, and communicate thought. It must not be treated as an evidentiary authority. Recent evidence that unguarded AI scaffolding can degrade unaided performance, homogenize output, and atrophy metacognition motivates the framework's insistence on friction, verification, and human authority over action. This conceptual paper defines the framework, locates it in adjacent literature — including Peircean abduction, the Geneplore model, divergent/convergent thinking, design thinking, extended-mind and distributed-cognition accounts, and contemporary research on AI cognitive scaffolding — proposes applications in education and work, outlines cautious mental-health-adjacent uses, presents four retrospective case narratives as process illustrations rather than validation, and develops falsifiable research propositions. Particular attention is given to cross-neurotype communication as an application hypothesis: an AI-mediated validation layer may help a person preserve an idiosyncratic path of discovery while translating the resulting argument into a form others can inspect. A final section sketches a future direction — the framework's procedural specification as a control policy for AI agent architectures — supported by a first literature audit, which found no verified system combining the architecture's seven elements; it is offered as a provisional research hypothesis, not a novelty claim. The paper concludes that Steve's Law is best treated as a working theory and research program. Its value depends on whether controlled studies show improvements in idea diversity, evidentiary quality, calibration, communication, and action without unacceptable increases in error, dependence, masking pressure, or cognitive burden.

items.title: Accountability and Transparency in AI Systems: A Human Rights Perspective
items.abstract: The proliferation of artificial intelligence across public and private sectors has positioned algorithmic decision-making at the heart of consequential outcomes, from criminal sentencing and credit scoring to healthcare allocation and employment screening. Yet the opacity of AI systems, combined with fragmented governance structures, has created a significant accountability deficit that threatens the realisation of fundamental human rights. This paper addresses the central research question: to what extent do existing human rights legal frameworks impose enforceable accountability and transparency obligations on states and corporate actors deploying AI systems? Using a doctrinal legal analysis methodology, the paper systematically examines primary legal instruments, including the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, the EU AI Act, and UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, to assess their capacity to govern AI-driven decision-making in rights-sensitive contexts. With special reference to the Indian constitutional framework, anchored in the Supreme Court’s landmark recognition of privacy as a fundamental right in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017), and to the emerging architecture of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, the paper situates India’s governance challenges within the global accountability debate. The paper identifies critical governance gaps, including the absence of enforceable audit mechanisms, inadequate redress pathways for rights-affected individuals, and the difficulty of attributing legal responsibility across complex AI supply chains. It concludes by proposing a human rights-by-design governance model that embeds accountability and transparency obligations across the full AI lifecycle, offering a principled framework for reconciling technological innovation with fundamental rights protection.

items.title: Against speech liberalism for generative AI
items.abstract: Abstract Speech liberalism holds that the linguistic output of generative AI is continuous with human speech and should therefore be treated as meaningful in broadly the same way. Strong versions of this view take the fluent behaviour of chatbots to justify attributing genuine linguistic and cognitive agency, while nevertheless advocating caution when questions of moral or legal responsibility arise. I argue that this gives too much evidential weight to successful conversational interaction, where speaker intentions largely recede into the background. Once AI-generated speech contributes to serious harm, however, those intentions become central. More broadly, the paper challenges a way of theorising about AI speech that builds classifications of linguistic agency primarily from successful conversational interaction. I develop two independent but complementary arguments. The first is ethical–legal. I argue that classifying chatbot output as speech is not normatively neutral: within existing free-speech doctrine, it risks generating responsibility and liability gaps in cases of AI-mediated harm. The second is epistemic. I argue that the behavioural evidence supporting strong speech liberalism is systematically distorted by anthropomorphic bias, reinforced by AI design practices. The paper concludes that theories of AI speech should not be built exclusively from successful conversational exchanges and that, until a broader evidential case is made, a more conservative approach to AI speech is warranted in high-stakes contexts.

items.title: AI -Generated Works And Copyright - Who Owns The Creativity? A Critical Analysis
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (ai) has transformed the creative landscape by generating literary works, painting, music, software code, and others form of artistic expression with minimal or no direct human intervention. These various new development challenges the traditional principles of copyright law, which is basically based on the assumption the creativity originates from a human author. As ai systems increasingly participate in the creative process, these questions lies at the heart of the evolving global and distinctly Indian, legal debate on ai-generated works and the future authorship, ownership, and accountability in the age of artificial intelligence. This paper synthesizes whether ai-generated works should receive copyright protection and if so then who should be recognized as the legal owner. Legally the study analyses the copyright act, 1957, international copyright instruments such as the WIPO copyright treaty, the trips agreement, the berne convention, and compares legal approaches adopted in India the United States, the United Kingdom, the European union, and China. It further evaluates landmark judicial decisions that have shaped the debate on originality and authorship in relation to emerging technologies. The paper argues that existing copyright laws are inadequate to address the unique challenges posed by autonomous ai systems. While jurisdiction differ in their treatment of ai- generated works, there remains no universally accepted legal framework governing ownership and protection. The study recommends legislative reforms that preserve incentives for innovation while maintaining the fundamental principle that copyright exists to encourage human creativity. It concludes that carefully balanced legal reforms are essential to ensure certainty, fairness, and sustainable development in the evolving digital economy.

items.title: AI ‐Mediated Multimodal Reading Education for EFL Learners: Effects on Students' Enjoyment and Engagement
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly reshaped educational practices by expanding opportunities for adaptive, multimodal and learner‐centered instruction. While growing attention has been paid to AI‐supported language learning, less is known about how multimodal AI technologies may support the emotional and behavioural dimensions of education among at‐risk students, particularly in second/foreign language reading contexts. Addressing this gap, the present study examined whether AI‐mediated multimodal reading education could enhance at‐risk English as a foreign language (EFL) learners' enjoyment and engagement during reading instruction. Using an interventional pre‐test/post‐test design, 80 at‐risk EFL students were assigned to either a control group ( n = 40) or an experimental group ( n = 40). Over two semesters, students in the experimental group received reading instruction supported by multimodal AI reading bots and AI chatbots, whereas those in the control group received conventional reading instruction. Enjoyment and engagement questionnaires were administered at the beginning and end of the intervention. ANCOVA results showed that students in the AI‐mediated education group demonstrated significantly higher levels of enjoyment and engagement than their counterparts in the control group. These findings suggest that multimodal AI technologies can contribute to more inclusive and emotionally supportive reading education for at‐risk learners. The study offers implications for educational researchers, teachers and policymakers seeking to integrate AI technologies into equitable and engaging language education.

items.title: AI Systems for Filmmaking: A Survey of HCI Research from a Labor-Centered Perspective
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is integrated into filmmaking and has attracted attention in human-computer interaction (HCI). Existing studies have primarily characterized AI systems for filmmaking by their capabilities and supported tasks, with limited attention to the organisation of filmmaking labor during system use. We review 31 HCI system papers and develop a three-layer taxonomy of labor sites, labor types, and human-AI allocation, examining where AI systems are positioned, what types of labor are involved during system use, and how those labor types are allocated between humans and AI. Our analysis reveals a concentration on individual below-the-line contexts, increasing attention to structural and meaning-making labor beyond execution, comparatively limited relational labor, and substantial variation in human-AI allocation across labor types. We further identify opportunities for the design and evaluation of AI systems that account for the broader organization of filmmaking labor. This review provides a labor-centered taxonomy for synthesizing AI systems for filmmaking and a basis for examining how AI may become involved in broader organizations of creative labor.

items.title: AI-Guided Stimulus and Debug Triage: A Methodology for Accelerating Pre-Silicon Emulation of Flagship SoC Programs
items.abstract: Raw emulation capacity for flagship system-on-chip (SoC) programs keeps growing, and engineer-hour supply keeps falling further behind it. That gap, not machine availability, is the actual bottleneck in pre-silicon verification today, driven by workload diversity across artificial intelligence (AI), extended reality (XR), and mobile platforms converging on a single die. This article argues that closing the gap requires a bounded, governed layer of AI-guided assistance rather than either extreme - full automation or continued reliance on engineer-only throughput. A three-layer adoption framework is proposed: scoping, which restricts AI involvement to stimulus generation for known-workload classes and anomaly-flagged debug triage while keeping root-cause sign-off and tape-out risk calls fully engineer-owned; validation, which requires every AI-generated output to be checked against a trusted reference - simulation, formal methods, or historical regression baselines - before an engineer may act on it; and governance, an operating-review cadence with rollback criteria defined before deployment, not improvised afterward. Pilot deployment of emulation-friendly RTL on a premium-tier mobile SoC program produced a shift of approximately 60 percent of RTL earlier in the program schedule, with no coverage-model exception granted to reach that outcome. The finding that emerges is not that AI accelerates verification - that much is already argued elsewhere - but that the acceleration only survives contact with a tape-out schedule when it is deliberately bounded. Emulation productivity under AI assistance is a governance problem before it is a technical one, and the three-layer framework is offered as a transferable operating model for programs where the cost of an unvalidated miss is unacceptable.

items.title: AI-in-the-human-loop: an operational model for mature human-AI collaboration
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models are powerful tools but come with risks and caveats for proper usage. In this work, we are concerned with effective human-AI collaboration. As in any team, it is key that all team members properly understand the problem at hand, the environment, and each other. In order to scaffold a mature human-AI collaboration, we propose a process framework based on continual, proactive, bidirectional assessment, fostering co-evolution of the human-AI team. While most research has focused on assessing the strengths and limitations of AI agents, we especially focus on the risks associated with a lack of maturity on the human side. The core idea is to have AI agents help humans assess themselves and to anticipate interaction issues. Furthermore, to place the proposal within a broader vision, we advance two novel concepts: (i) “AI-in-the-human-loop”, the idea of AI agents observing and acting within human reasoning and activity, and (ii) “human-under-test”, a software testing analogy that suggests techniques for assessing human maturity by AI agents. A case study of a human-AI team involved in a statistical analysis project is considered, and analysed through an LLM-as-a-judge setup. Preliminary results highlight collaboration maturity issues and the possibility of proactive corrections, showcasing limitations in current collaborative workflows and opportunities for further research.

items.title: AI, DEEPFAKES, AND DEMOCRATIC ACCOUNTABILITY: THE ROLE OF RTI LAWS
items.abstract: With the advent of artificial intelligence and deepfake technologies, the modern information landscape is changing, giving rise to realistic synthetic text, images, audio, and videos. Such changes pose significant problems for democratic accountability, because they can skew political discourse, reduce trust in authentic information and make it difficult to attribute responsibility. Generative AI, deepfakes, and the Right to Information (RTI) and Freedom of Information (FOI) laws, along with current AI governance frameworks, are explored in this narrative review. Relevant policy and regulatory instruments were discussed in conjunction with literature from 2017 to 2025 across legal, technological, political, and public-administration fields. The review highlights ongoing challenges with the current RTI and FOI frameworks, such as the opacity of algorithms, proprietary systems, the ambiguity of AI-generated records, explainability issues, and challenges with verifying synthetic content. Comparative governance developments show a shift toward proactive disclosure, documentation, risk assessment, human oversight, and authentication requirements. Building on these findings, the article proposes an integrated AI–RTI framework centred on access, authenticity, traceability, explainability, and accountability. The framework repositions RTI from a primarily disclosure-oriented mechanism toward a broader democratic verification infrastructure supporting trustworthy public information, institutional responsibility, citizen scrutiny, and accountable governance in increasingly AI-mediated information environments while complementing platform regulation and technological safeguards.
